rv.q: Perhaps this ‘Camelot’ is a manifestation practice for Sorkin, one that bolsters egalitarian rulers who value love and mercy just as highly as power and might...Genial heroes are needed to move us forward.
The revival makes you want to believe in a great musical called Camelot, even if such a thing never did exist.
This new Theater production of Lerner and Loewe's Camelot is a thoughtful, beautifully mounted revival that brings fresh perspective to the classic musical while honoring its legacy.
As beautifully sung as this new Camelot is – and it is – the production nearly scuttles romance along with the magic.
It moves like a funeral procession for itself.
What remains is a cooler “Camelot,” with its own head-scratching dramaturgy.

Neither, it seems, is sufficient today.
It’s the chilliest “Camelot” you ever did see and it embodies so many of the current neuroses surrounding the revival of classic American musicals.

Reinvigorated by Sorkin — who has long painted a dreamy, egalitarian view of politics within his works — and his new book, the musical succeeds in evoking that dream for one brief, shining moment once again.
Indeed, this Camelot, which I admittedly could not muster up much enthusiasm for upon entering the Theater, was surprisingly engaging.
Camelot is a sweeping drama packed with royal romance and sword fights.

If this Camelot is a bit confused on whether it wants to be a majestic golden age musical or a gritty take on the shaky foundations of a monarchical ménage à trois, it pulls through on the strength of its cast, which tightly brings the work’s brief shining moment into glorious light.
So, it's a pleasure to report that Bartlett Sher's elegant revival is definitely a vast improvement.
And magic is exactly what this Camelot most obviously lacks.
So smoothed out has the story become that the actors – admirable all – can do little more than stay afloat.
It’s a shame that this “Camelot,” despite its shining moments and impeccable pedigree, doesn’t offer more of that kind of splendor.
It’s seldom exciting or joyful.
But, as entertaining as the musical numbers are, it’s hard not to be disappointed by this production.
For what it’s worth, all this talk of love in the final scene came as news to me.
Ultimately, though, this Camelot revival falls on its own sword with its reworked book.

Unfortunately, his new book (which removes all magical elements, turns Morgan Le Fey as a scientist, and questions how Arthur could have pulled the sword from the stone) is too clumsy and self-conscious in its attempt to draw contemporary parallels and critical viewpoints.
It is to be hoped that future musical revivals of golden age shows will either trust the original material or their audiences to know that things were different in earlier decades.
Due to Sorkin’s undernourished scribing, the emotions the songs reveal don’t fit the emotion-deprived characters.
Camelot remains as disjointed as before.
The result is arid, a musical that can't decide why anyone is singing.
At almost three hours on a spartan stage, it grinds into a numbingly boring show.
The result is Sorkin’s retrofitted play, where mostly incongruous songs with erudite lyrics infrequently pop in.
I could not help but fall for its simplistic charms and excellent ensemble cast.
I'm afraid most of the blame for this revisal's failings have to be laid at Sorkin's door.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Sorkin's magic-free "Camelot" revival: some praise the lush score and talented cast, but many find his updated book removes enchantment, leaving a somber, overlong production that lacks the romance and fun of the original.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
